1.pericope_label: The ark seven months in Philistia; the priests and diviners; the trespass offering

schools.summary: Prefer country to field while reporting the alternative, date the capture by counting back from harvest, correct Josephus on the length of the captivity, and canvass what the golden images were, down to the rabbinic reading of them as talismans.
Use the field reading to account for the plague of mice unrecorded in the previous chapter, and measure the loss as Israel’s, seven months punished by the absence of the ark.

Supply the practice of ancient divination and of votive offerings where the text assumes it, judge the Philistines to have conceived Israel’s God as a capricious tribal deity, and defend the priests’ knowledge of the Exodus as unremarkable.

Admit ignorance of what divination actually consisted in; find in the impulse to send gifts a principle common to all nations and endorsed by the law; and defend the offerers’ motive as humiliation rather than mockery.

debates: Whether in the field means the open country where the ark was abandoned (Procopius, and the inference Henry builds on it) or simply the territory of the Philistines (Gill and Henry’s own preference, with the Targum).
How long the ark was in Philistia — seven months by the text, four by Josephus, whom Gill corrects.
What the Philistines supposed they were placating: a capricious deity of their own kind (Ellicott) or a God whose claims they dimly and rightly perceived (Gill, Clarke).
What the golden images represented — the cities, the whole man, the diseased part, or talismans made to carry away the disease (Maimonides, in Gill).
outliers: Clarke alone confesses that what divination consisted in is unknown.
Ellicott alone follows the custom of votive images from pagan antiquity into Christian churches and into modern practice.
Ellicott alone notes that the mice enter the Hebrew text here but stand earlier in the Greek.

7.pericope_label: The new cart, the two milch kine, and the test

schools.summary: Ground the new cart in the meaning of sanctification, call the trial complete on two independent grounds, and expound chance from the Hebrew and the English alike as an event of concurring natural causes still wholly within the divine government.
Explain the cart by the absence of Levites before appealing to the ark’s honour, and keep to what the lords were directed to observe.

Report the reverence shown as a right feeling while passing on a rival explanation from the virtue of new things; set out both branches of the test and the diviners’ own expectation; and contrast Philistine awe with Israelite carelessness to come.

debates: Why the cart was new: because what has served common use may not serve God (Clarke), because no Levites were at hand to carry the ark and honour required a new vehicle (Gill), or because new things were supposed to have a peculiar virtue (the Speaker’s Commentary, reported by Ellicott alongside the reverent explanation).
What the Philistine priests expected the test to show — Ellicott alone says they were confident the cows would go home, and therefore that the plague would prove natural.
Whether chance names something outside divine government — denied at length by Clarke, who redefines the word from its roots in two languages.
outliers: Clarke alone derives the English chance from the French and connects it with the legal term escheat.
Clarke alone objects that jewels mistranslates a word meaning vessels or implements.
Ellicott alone anticipates the fate of the men of Bethshemesh in order to sharpen the Philistines’ reverence.

10.pericope_label: The Philistines send the ark away; the kine take the straight way to Bethshemesh

schools.summary: Read the return as a second exodus — no ransom taken, gold given to be rid of it — and draw the rule that God takes honour from those who seek to dishonour him.
Find the proof in the lowing, which shows the natural instinct persisting while the behaviour contradicts it; note the crossroads and the lords’ personal attendance as guards against imposture.
Argue from the plainness of the narrative itself to its truth, and follow the arrival, the great stone, the burnt offering and the Levites’ handling of the ark in order.
Observe that Philistines handled the ark unpunished where an Israelite was afterwards struck for it.

debates: Whether the cart was deliberately set at a fork between the road to Ekron and the road to Bethshemesh — reported by Clarke as the view of some.
What the lowing signifies: the cows calling for their calves (Clarke) or, more precisely, evidence that instinct was overborne rather than removed (Wesley).
Why the Philistine lords accompanied the cart to the border — to prevent imposture (Wesley) or to secure the fullest conviction of God’s interposition (Clarke).
outliers: Henry alone aligns the ark’s return point by point with the exodus, down to the gold given to speed its departure.
Gill alone contrasts the unpunished Philistines with Uzzah.
Ellicott alone rests a case for the narrative’s authenticity on its unadorned style.

13.pericope_label: The reapers of Bethshemesh; the great stone; the five golden emerods

schools.summary: Concede a double irregularity in the sacrifice — female victims and an unchosen place — and excuse it only by the extraordinary case; explain the destruction of cart and cattle by their having passed out of secular use.

Deny any irregularity, since the ark’s presence made the place lawful; read the priestly character of Bethshemesh as explaining the disaster to come; and infer that the ark rested in all five cities though only three are named.

Read the notice about the Levites as a pluperfect, identify them as priests, and note that the city belonged to the very Kohathites charged with carrying the ark; date the harvest so as to supply the crowd of witnesses.

debates: Whether the sacrifice broke the law: a double error excusable only by necessity (Wesley) or no transgression at all, the ark’s presence sanctifying the place (Ellicott).
Why the cows were killed and the cart burnt — as a thank-offering of joy (Keil) or because neither could be returned to common use (Clarke).
Whether those who took down the ark were priests or Levites strictly so called — Gill insists on priests, Clarke is content with Levites.
Who Joshua the Bethshemite was — unknown, and Gill will not decide whether he was a Levite.
outliers: Ellicott alone treats the whole episode as an indictment of a priesthood that had forfeited its office, and reads the coming judgement as unsurprising in consequence.
Gill alone notes that Bethshemesh belonged to the Kohathites, whose charge was the ark itself.

19.pericope_label: The men of Bethshemesh smitten; the ark sent to Kirjath-jearim

schools.summary: Defend the received number by widening the population; treat the curiosity as natural though culpable; and read the cry as blame-shifting, a standing habit of consciences under terror.

Judge the Hebrew figure corrupt and show how the versions divide it; reconstruct the offence as drunken irreverence by the priestly chief men, while rejecting a rendering that would soften it; and find in the survivors’ superstition a real conviction of sin that anticipates Samuel’s reformation.

Leave the cry open between complaint and reverence, and add that no one can stand except through the mercy seat; give positive reasons for the choice of Kirjath-jearim while leaving Shiloh’s fate undecided.
Explain the offence from the psychology of the forbidden, and distinguish the pretext of checking the tables from the real motive of prying into what God had concealed.

debates: Whether the text’s fifty thousand and seventy can stand: corrupt or interpolated (Clarke, Ellicott), or defensible if the people means those gathered from all parts (Wesley).
What the offence was: natural curiosity (Wesley), curiosity about the forbidden dressed in a pretext (Henry), or drunken irreverence in the priestly leaders (Ellicott).
Whether the Hebrew means looked into the ark or merely stared at it — Ellicott reports the second and rejects it.
Whether who is able to stand is an evasion that blames God (Clarke, Wesley), a reverent confession (Gill’s alternative), or superstition containing genuine conviction (Ellicott).
Why Kirjath-jearim rather than Shiloh — because Shiloh was already destroyed (Clarke), or for reasons of safety and standing, with Shiloh’s fate left open (Gill, Wesley).
outliers: Ellicott alone attributes the sacrilege to men heated with wine, and alone reads the aftermath as the seed of Samuel’s reformation.
Henry alone observes that the ark’s concealment was itself what provoked the desire to see it.
